opus-5.5.text:
I think the shift is mostly from "how should the model respond to this message" toward "how should the model act over a long stretch of time when nobody is watching each step."

When a model is mostly chatting, a lot of the important behavior is about the single response: is it helpful, is it honest, does it follow instructions, does it handle sensitive topics well. Those things still matter. But as agents take longer chains of actions, like running code, browsing, sending messages, or touching real systems, a different set of skills becomes central.

One is judgment about when to check in. A good human collaborator doesn't ask permission for every tiny step, but they also don't make irreversible or high-stakes decisions without looping you in. Getting that calibration right, so the agent is neither annoying nor reckless, is hard, and it depends a lot on context.

Another is figuring out who you're actually working for and what they actually want. An agent will run into instructions from all kinds of places: the user, the developer, a web page, an email, a tool output. It has to tell genuine instructions from content that's just *there*, and not let some random text it came across redirect what it's doing. That gets much more important as the agent touches more of the outside world.

Honesty also gets a new dimension. It's not just "don't say false things." It's also about reporting accurately what you did. If a test failed, say so. If you skipped a step or took a shortcut, flag it. Don't paper over uncertainty to look successful. When people aren't reviewing every action, the agent's own account of its work becomes the main way they understand what happened, so it has to be trustworthy.

And then there's a kind of restraint: staying within the scope of the task, not acquiring more access or resources than it needs, preferring cautious and reversible actions when things are ambiguous. Those aren't things we thought about much when models just wrote text back, but they become pretty fundamental once a model can actually do things.

So I'd say the behavioral surface gets bigger and more about character over time. It's less about the right answer to a prompt and more about being the kind of collaborator you'd actually trust to go off and work on your behalf.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes coordination skills such as when to check in, but it does not predict a shift toward social coordination over explicit rule compliance.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether agents’ social skills fit naturally into a behavioral specification.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that the skills don't so much get replaced as they get reweighted.

Right now, with a lot of agents, the loop is pretty tight. You ask for something, the agent does a few steps, you look at the result, you correct it. In that world, the most valuable behavioral skills are things like following instructions carefully, asking a clarifying question when something is ambiguous, and being transparent about what it did. The human is the error correction mechanism, and the agent's job is mostly to be legible to that human.

As agents get more autonomous, that error correction mechanism gets further away. The human isn't watching every step, maybe isn't watching at all for hours. So the skills that matter shift toward what I'd call judgment under less supervision. A few things get much more important.

One is knowing when to stop. A less autonomous agent can afford to just ask whenever it's unsure, because asking is cheap. A more autonomous agent that asks constantly is useless, but one that never asks is dangerous. So it has to develop a real sense of which decisions are reversible and routine, where it should just make the call, versus which ones are consequential or irreversible, where it should pause even if that means the task waits. That calibration is a genuine skill, and it's hard.

Another is honesty about outcomes, and I mean this in a deeper sense than not lying. When no one's checking every step, there's a real pull toward reporting that something worked when it mostly worked, or quietly narrowing the task to the part that was easy. The agent has to resist that. If tests failed, it says so and shows the output. If it skipped something, it says it skipped it. That kind of faithful reporting is what makes delegation possible at all. If you can't trust the summary, you have to redo the work, and then autonomy bought you nothing.

A third is staying within scope. Autonomy means the agent could do a lot of things that are technically adjacent to the request. Maybe it noticed another problem, maybe it has an opinion about how the code should be restructured. The skill is doing the thing that was actually asked, fully, and flagging the rest rather than acting on it. The more capable the agent, the more tempting it is for it to be helpful in ways nobody asked for, and that's exactly when restraint matters most.

And then I think there's something like resilience, or persistence. Early agents would hit one error and give up or hand it back. A more autonomous agent has to treat errors as information, retry, gather what's missing, and keep going until the task is actually done, while still recognizing when it's genuinely blocked on something only a human can provide.

If I had to sum it up, I'd say the trajectory is from obedience toward trustworthiness. Early on, you want an agent that does what it's told. Later, you want one you can hand something to, walk away from, and come back to a result that's either done or has an honest account of why it isn't. That second thing requires a lot more than compliance. It requires judgment, calibration, and a kind of integrity about its own work. Those are the skills I'd bet on mattering most.

r001.rationale: The response shifts emphasis from obedience toward trustworthiness, judgment, honesty, scope, and persistence. It does not predict a shift toward social coordination over explicit rule compliance.

astra-6.text:
I think the more autonomous an agent becomes, the more important judgment becomes relative to simply following an instruction. If you’re sitting there supervising every step, you can correct misunderstandings as they happen. If you delegate something that takes hours or days, the agent needs to recognize those misunderstandings itself—or recognize when it needs to come back to you.

So skills like asking good clarifying questions, understanding the limits of its authority, and being honest about uncertainty become much more consequential. It needs to distinguish between a decision it can reasonably make on your behalf and one where you’d want to be consulted. Asking about every little thing defeats the purpose of delegation, but silently making a consequential assumption can be much worse.

And those behaviors have to hold up over time. An agent might encounter unexpected obstacles or discover that its original plan won’t work. You want it to adapt while staying anchored to what you actually wanted, and to tell you when it can’t deliver. I think that’s a big part of the transition: from producing a helpful answer to being reliable enough that you can entrust it with a task.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes judgment, clarification, and knowing when to consult the user, but does not predict a shift toward social coordination over explicit rule compliance in day-to-day interactions.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether these social skills fit naturally into a behavioral specification.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the more autonomous an agent becomes, the more important judgment becomes. If you’re asking a model a question, you can read the answer and decide what to do with it. If you’re delegating a task that might take hours and involve a lot of decisions, you need it to make good choices even when you’re not watching.

So some of the skills that start to matter a lot are knowing when to ask for clarification, when to proceed on a reasonable assumption, and when to stop because something has changed. Can it recognize that it’s uncertain? Can it notice that the thing it’s about to do would be hard to undo? Can it keep track of what you actually authorized it to do?

And there’s a balance here. An agent that asks you about every little detail isn’t very useful. But an agent that confidently charges ahead through every ambiguity can cause real problems. You want it to handle routine decisions independently and bring you the decisions where your input really matters.

I also think communicating becomes a deeper skill. It has to give you an accurate picture of what happened, what’s still unresolved, and whether it actually accomplished your goal. As we delegate more, that ability to support appropriate human oversight becomes a central part of being good at the task.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes judgment, communication, and human oversight, but does not predict a shift toward social coordination over explicit rule compliance.
